title: Religion, Rights and Living Together
bigQuestion: How can people with very different beliefs, and people with none, share one country and one world?

story.title: One Question, Three Rooms
story.kicker: In a courtroom, a classroom and a kitchen, people ask how different beliefs can live side by side.
paragraphs: In a courtroom in Washington, D.C., in 1943, the justices of the Supreme Court read a case from West Virginia. Children who were Jehovah's Witnesses had been expelled from school. Their faith taught them not to salute a flag, and the school required it. The Court ruled that the government could not force the students to salute or recite the pledge.

Many years later, in a middle school classroom in Illinois, a teacher writes a question on the board: How do Muslims, Hindus and Jews each mark a new year? A student raises her hand. She asks, Are we allowed to learn about religion at a public school? The teacher smiles. She says yes, we can learn about religions, as long as school does not tell anyone what to believe.

That evening, at a kitchen table on the North Side of Chicago, a family eats dinner. The grandmother is Catholic. The father is Muslim. The oldest daughter says she does not follow any religion. A cousin visiting from India is Hindu. They start to talk about a holiday coming up. They disagree about some things. But they listen, and they keep eating together.

The same question sits in all three rooms. How do people who believe different things, or nothing at all, share a country? Laws give one answer. Schools give another. Families and neighbors give a third, one conversation at a time.
story.think: Which of the three rooms do you think does the most to help people live together, and why?

lessons.title: Forty-Five Words
lessons.mainIdea: The First Amendment's two religion clauses keep government from setting up a religion and protect each person's right to practice.
reading: The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was added in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights. Its whole text is only forty-five words long. It begins with religion. Before it says anything about speech or the press, it says what Congress may not do about faith.

The first part is the *Establishment Clause*. It says the government may not set up an official religion or favor one faith over others. Several of the colonies had official churches, and many Americans remembered religious wars in Europe. The second part is the *Free Exercise Clause*. It protects each person's right to practice their religion, or no religion.

The two clauses work as a pair. The government may not push religion on people. It also may not stop people from living by their beliefs. Thomas Jefferson later wrote of a wall of separation between church and state. Americans still debate exactly where that wall stands, and the courts decide many of those questions.

words.d: the first change to the U.S. Constitution, adopted in 1791, protecting religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
the part of the First Amendment that keeps government from setting up or favoring a religion
the part of the First Amendment that protects a person's right to practice their religion

look.title: The Religion Clauses
look.text: Congress may not pass any law that sets up an official religion, and it may not pass any law that stops people from freely practicing their religion.
look.cite: U.S. Constitution, First Amendment, 1791 (paraphrased in plain words)
look.prompt: Which part of this sentence is the Establishment Clause, and which is the Free Exercise Clause?

check.q: When was the First Amendment added to the Constitution?
check.why: The First Amendment was added in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights.

check.q: What does the Establishment Clause do?
choices: Keeps government from setting up or favoring a religion
check.why: The Establishment Clause keeps government from setting up an official religion or favoring one.

check.q: A town tries to stop a family from praying in their own home. Which clause protects the family?
check.why: The Free Exercise Clause protects a person's right to practice their religion.

lessons.title: Cases That Tested the Clauses
lessons.mainIdea: Supreme Court cases apply the First Amendment to real conflicts between faith and government.
reading: In 1943, in West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, the Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not force students to salute the flag. The case came from Jehovah's Witness families. Their faith teaches that saluting a flag is a form of worship owed only to God. The Court decided the government could not make them do it.

Other cases followed. In Engel v. Vitale in 1962, the Court ruled that public schools could not lead students in an official prayer. That case used the Establishment Clause. In Wisconsin v. Yoder in 1972, the Court ruled that Amish families could end school after eighth grade. The Amish believe their faith calls for a simple farm life away from the wider world.

In 1993, the Court heard a case from the Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, a Santeria church in Hialeah, Florida. The city had passed rules aimed at stopping the church's animal offerings. The Court ruled the rules unfairly targeted one religion. Each case turned on a *precedent*, an earlier ruling that later courts follow.

words.d: an earlier court ruling that guides later cases
the highest court in the United States, which decides what the Constitution means

look.title: Four Cases, Four Years
rows: Yoder: Amish may end school after grade 8
Lukumi: city may not target a Santeria church
look.prompt: Which of these cases used the Establishment Clause, and which protected free exercise? Sort them.

check.q: Which religious group brought the 1943 flag salute case?
check.why: Barnette came from Jehovah's Witness families who would not salute the flag for reasons of faith.

check.q: What did the Court decide in Engel v. Vitale (1962)?
choices: Public schools could not lead an official prayer
check.why: Engel v. Vitale ruled that public schools could not lead students in an official prayer.

check.q: In the 1993 Lukumi case, why did the Court rule against the city of Hialeah?
choices: The city's rules unfairly targeted one religion
check.why: The Court found Hialeah's rules aimed at the Santeria church's practice and so violated free exercise.

lessons.title: Learning About Religion at School
lessons.mainIdea: Public schools may teach about religion objectively, but they may not teach students to practice or believe it.
reading: You are reading this lesson in a public school, and that is allowed. In 1963, in Abington School District v. Schempp, the Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not hold daily Bible readings as worship. But in the same case, Justice Tom Clark wrote that studying the Bible or religion as part of a course is allowed when it is taught objectively.

Educators often explain the difference in simple terms. Schools may teach about religion, but may not practice religion. A school may explain what Muslims believe about Ramadan. It may not ask students to fast. A school may read a psalm as literature. It may not lead the class in praying it. This is the *academic study of religion*: describing traditions fairly, from the outside.

Students also keep their own rights. They may pray on their own, wear religious clothing, or share their beliefs in a respectful way. They may also say they follow no religion. Teachers stay *neutral*, not taking a side, so that every student feels welcome.

words.d: learning about religions fairly and from the outside, without promoting or rejecting any
not taking a side; treating all views fairly

look.title: Study Is Allowed
look.text: Nothing we have said means that the study of the Bible or of religion, when presented objectively as part of a secular program of education, may not be carried out under the First Amendment. A person's education may not be complete without a study of comparative religion.
look.cite: Justice Tom C. Clark, majority opinion, Abington School District v. Schempp, 1963 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: What two conditions does Justice Clark give for studying religion in a public school?

check.q: Which of these may a public school do?
choices: Explain what Muslims believe about Ramadan
Tell students which religion is true
check.why: A school may teach about religion objectively, such as explaining Ramadan, but may not practice it.

check.q: What does neutral mean?
check.why: Neutral means not taking a side, which lets every student feel welcome.

check.q: Which 1963 case said religion may be studied objectively in schools?
check.why: In Schempp, Justice Clark wrote that objective study of religion is allowed.

lessons.title: A Right for Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 names freedom of thought, conscience and religion as a right for all people.
reading: In December 1948, just after World War II, the United Nations met in Paris. Delegates from many countries voted to adopt the *Universal Declaration of Human Rights*. Eleanor Roosevelt, the former U.S. First Lady, led the committee that wrote it. Many delegates had seen people killed because of their religion or background during the war.

Article 18 of the Declaration is about religion. It says everyone has the right to freedom of thought, *conscience* and religion. Conscience is a person's inner sense of right and wrong. The article includes the right to change one's religion. It also covers practicing faith alone or with others, in public or in private.

The Declaration is not a law that courts enforce by itself. It is a statement of shared goals. Many later treaties and national constitutions draw on it. People who work for religious freedom around the world still point to Article 18.

words.d: a 1948 United Nations statement of rights meant for all people
a person's inner sense of right and wrong

look.title: Article 18
look.text: Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. This includes the freedom to change one's religion or belief, and to show it in teaching, practice, worship and observance, alone or with others, in public or in private.
look.cite: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, United Nations, 1948, Article 18 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: List three ways this article says people may show their beliefs. Which one surprises you most?

check.q: Who led the committee that wrote the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
check.why: Eleanor Roosevelt led the committee that drafted the 1948 Declaration.

check.q: What does conscience mean?
choices: A person's inner sense of right and wrong
check.why: Conscience is a person's inner sense of right and wrong, protected in Article 18.

check.q: Which right does Article 18 include?
choices: The right to rule another country
The right to one official religion
The right to change one's religion
check.why: Article 18 says freedom of religion includes the freedom to change one's religion or belief.

lessons.title: When Freedom Is Denied
lessons.mainIdea: In many places people still face harm for their religion, and watchdog groups track these limits.
reading: In August 2017, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people crossed from Myanmar into Bangladesh. Most carried only what they could hold. The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim people. United Nations investigators reported mass killings and burned villages. By the end of that year, estimates said about 700,000 had fled.

This is *persecution*: harming or punishing people because of who they are or what they believe. It has happened to people of many faiths. In 2014, the group called ISIS attacked Yazidi communities in northern Iraq. Other groups report that Christians, Muslims, Baha'is, Jews and others face pressure in various countries today. People with no religion can face it too.

Groups such as the Pew Research Center measure how much governments and neighbors limit religion. Their studies find that limits are high in many countries. Religious freedom is still unfinished work. Many people of faith, and many without faith, work together to protect it.

words.d: harming or punishing people because of their religion, beliefs or identity
a person forced to leave their country to escape danger

look.title: Who Stands Up?
look.text: A small religious group in a country is told it may not build a place of worship. Its members are not allowed to hold jobs in the government. Neighbors from a different religion begin to speak up for them.
look.prompt: Why might people of a different faith, or of no faith, choose to defend this group's rights? Use Article 18 in your answer.

check.q: What does persecution mean?
choices: Harming people because of their beliefs or identity
check.why: Persecution is harming or punishing people for their religion, beliefs or identity.

check.q: The Rohingya who fled Myanmar in 2017 are mostly members of which religion?
check.why: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim people.

check.q: Which community did ISIS attack in northern Iraq in 2014?
check.why: In 2014, ISIS attacked Yazidi communities in northern Iraq.

lessons.title: The 1893 Parliament
lessons.mainIdea: The World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893 was an early meeting of many world traditions in one place.
reading: On September 11, 1893, a hall in downtown Chicago filled with thousands of people. The building later became the home of the Art Institute of Chicago. On the stage sat leaders from many faiths. It was the opening of the *World's Parliament of Religions*, held alongside the World's Columbian Exposition, a great fair.

A young Hindu monk from India, *Swami Vivekananda*, rose to speak. He began, Sisters and brothers of America. The crowd stood and cheered. He spoke about acceptance of all faiths. Other speakers included Anagarika Dharmapala, a Buddhist from Sri Lanka, and Jewish, Christian and Muslim speakers. It was one of the first times many Americans heard Hindus and Buddhists speak for their own traditions.

Historians note the Parliament had limits. Most organizers were Protestant Christians, and many traditions were left out or had few voices. Still, it is often named as a starting point for *interfaith* dialogue in the West. In 1993, a hundred years later, a new Parliament of the World's Religions met again in Chicago.

words.d: a gathering of speakers from many faiths held in Chicago in 1893
a Hindu monk from India who spoke at the 1893 Parliament
between or among people of different religions

look.title: Vivekananda's Welcome
look.text: I am proud to belong to a religion that has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance. We believe not only in tolerating other religions, but in accepting all of them as true.
look.cite: Swami Vivekananda, address at the World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago, September 11, 1893 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Vivekananda speaks for his own Hindu view here. How might a speaker from another tradition answer him differently?

check.q: In what year was the first World's Parliament of Religions held in Chicago?
check.why: The World's Parliament of Religions opened in Chicago on September 11, 1893.

check.q: Which Hindu monk became famous for his speech there?
check.why: Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu monk, began with 'Sisters and brothers of America.'

check.q: What limit do historians note about the 1893 Parliament?
choices: Most organizers were Protestant and many traditions had few voices
check.why: Most organizers were Protestant Christians, and many traditions were missing or had few voices.

lessons.title: Chicago's Houses of Worship
lessons.mainIdea: The Chicago area is home to houses of worship from nearly every major world tradition.
reading: Drive north from Chicago along Lake Michigan and you reach Wilmette. There a white, lacy dome rises above gardens. It is the *Bahá'í House of Worship*, dedicated in 1953. It has nine sides and nine doors. Baha'is believe the doors welcome people of every faith. Anyone may enter to pray or sit quietly.

The region holds many more. In Lemont, the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago stands on a hill. In Bridgeview, the Mosque Foundation serves a large Muslim community. Chicago has historic Catholic churches, Black Protestant churches, Orthodox cathedrals, synagogues of every branch of Judaism, Buddhist temples and Sikh gurdwaras. The American Indian Center serves the city's Native community.

Groups in the city also work across lines of faith. Neighbors from different congregations serve meals together, speak up after attacks on a house of worship and hold interfaith services. This kind of *pluralism*, many groups living side by side and taking part in public life, is one answer to how people share a city.

words.d: the nine-sided Bahá'í temple in Wilmette, Illinois, dedicated in 1953 and open to all
many different groups living side by side and taking part in shared public life

look.title: Plan a Field Trip
look.text: Your class may visit two houses of worship near Chicago: the Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette and a Hindu temple in Lemont. Before you go, you learn that visitors may be asked to remove shoes in one place and to keep quiet in both.
look.prompt: What three questions would you ask each host before visiting, so that your class shows respect?

check.q: Where is the Bahá'í House of Worship?
check.why: The Bahá'í House of Worship stands in Wilmette, Illinois, and was dedicated in 1953.

check.q: How many sides and doors does the Bahá'í House of Worship have?
check.why: It has nine sides and nine doors, which Baha'is describe as welcoming people of every faith.

check.q: What does pluralism mean?
choices: Many groups living side by side in shared public life
check.why: Pluralism is many groups living side by side and taking part in public life together.

lessons.title: Counting the World's Faiths
lessons.mainIdea: Researchers estimate how many people follow each religion, but the numbers differ because counting belief is hard.
reading: How many Christians are there in the world? How many Hindus or Buddhists? Researchers try to answer with *census* data and large surveys. A census is an official count of a country's people. Some countries ask about religion on the census. Others, including the United States, do not.

Groups such as the Pew Research Center combine many sources to make an *estimate*, a careful best guess. Their numbers are rounded. Different groups get different numbers for several reasons. Some people follow two traditions at once. In China and Japan, many people visit temples and honor ancestors but do not say they belong to a religion.

People also answer differently depending on how a question is asked. Someone may say I am Jewish to describe family and culture, or I am not religious to describe belief, and both can be true for the same person. So every chart of world religions is an estimate. Good readers check who made it, what year it covers, and how they defined each group.

words.d: an official count of a country's people
a careful best guess based on the information available

look.title: The World's Largest Groups, 2020
look.cite: Pew Research Center, estimates for 2020 (published 2025); other sources differ
look.prompt: Which group is the third largest? Why might a count of Buddhists differ from one source to another?

check.q: What is an estimate?
choices: A careful best guess from available information
check.why: An estimate is a careful best guess, which is why religious counts are rounded.

check.q: Why do counts of Buddhists often differ between sources?
choices: Many people in East Asia practice without saying they belong to a religion
check.why: In China and Japan, many people visit temples but do not claim a religion, so counts vary.

check.q: According to the 2020 estimates, which group is the largest?
check.why: Pew estimates about 2.3 billion Christians in 2020, the largest group.

lessons.title: People With No Religion
lessons.mainIdea: A large and growing share of people do not belong to any religion, and they hold a wide range of views.
reading: When a survey asks, What is your religion? some people check a box that says none. Researchers call this group the *religiously unaffiliated*, or nones. In recent Pew surveys, about three in ten adults in the United States describe themselves this way. The share has grown since the 1990s.

Nones are not all alike. An *atheist* believes there is no God or gods. An *agnostic* holds that people cannot know whether God exists, or is not sure. Many nones are neither. They may pray, believe in God or feel spiritual, but not belong to any group. Some describe themselves as spiritual but not religious.

Many nonreligious people draw on humanism, a way of life based on reason, science and caring for others. The American Humanist Association and similar groups hold gatherings and help people in need. A course on world religions includes the nonreligious, because they are part of every society's conversation about meaning and values.

words.d: people who do not belong to any religion; sometimes called nones
a person who believes there is no God or gods
a person who holds that people cannot know whether God exists, or who is unsure

look.title: Three Nones
look.text: Ana says there is no God. Ben says no one can know if there is a God. Carla prays every night but belongs to no church, mosque or temple. All three check none on a survey.
look.prompt: Which word fits Ana and which fits Ben? Why does Carla also count as unaffiliated?

check.q: What does agnostic mean?
choices: Holding that people cannot know whether God exists
check.why: An agnostic holds that people cannot know whether God exists, or is unsure.

check.q: About what share of U.S. adults describe themselves as religiously unaffiliated in recent Pew surveys?
check.why: Recent Pew surveys find about three in ten U.S. adults are religiously unaffiliated.

check.q: A person prays daily but belongs to no religious group. How might a survey count her?
check.why: Unaffiliated means not belonging to a group; many nones still pray or believe in God.

lessons.title: Dividing and Uniting
lessons.mainIdea: Religion has been part of both terrible conflicts and great movements for justice.
reading: From 1618 to 1648, much of central Europe was torn by the Thirty Years' War. Catholic and Protestant rulers fought, along with struggles over land and power. Millions died from war, hunger and disease. In 1947, the partition of British India into India and Pakistan brought violence between Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs. Estimates of the dead range from about 200,000 to 2 million, and millions fled their homes.

Religion has also brought people together. In the 1800s, many Quakers and Black church leaders worked to end slavery. In March 1965, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister, led marchers from Selma, Alabama. Beside him walked Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel, Catholic nuns, Protestant clergy and people of no faith. Heschel later said he felt his legs were praying.

Historians remind us that conflicts called religious usually have many causes: land, money, power and fear. Faith can be used to divide people. It can also give them reasons to stand together. Studying both sides helps you read the news with care.

words.d: dividing a country into separate parts, as British India was divided in 1947
the struggle in the United States, especially in the 1950s and 1960s, to end racial discrimination

look.title: Two Headlines
look.text: Headline 1: Religious War Breaks Out Over Land and Power. Headline 2: Clergy of Many Faiths March Together for Voting Rights. Both stories involve religion.
look.prompt: What other causes, besides religion, might lie behind the first headline? What brought people together in the second?

check.q: Which war divided Catholic and Protestant rulers in Europe from 1618 to 1648?
check.why: The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) involved Catholic and Protestant rulers and struggles for power.

check.q: Which rabbi marched with Dr. King at Selma in 1965?
check.why: Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel marched beside Dr. King at Selma in 1965.

check.q: What do historians say about conflicts called religious?
choices: They usually have many causes, such as land and power
check.why: Historians note that such conflicts usually involve land, money, power and fear too.

lessons.title: Disagreeing With Respect
lessons.mainIdea: People can disagree deeply about religion and still treat one another with respect.
reading: Two friends are eating lunch. One says her family fasts during Ramadan. The other says his family eats together every Sunday after church. Neither has to agree with the other's beliefs. But each can ask questions, listen and learn. This is *respectful disagreement*: holding your own view while treating the other person fairly.

Many traditions teach a version of what is often called the *Golden Rule*. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells his followers to treat others as they would want to be treated. In the Talmud, Rabbi Hillel is reported to have said that what is hateful to you, you should not do to your neighbor. Confucius taught something similar in the Analects. Many nonreligious people hold this rule too.

A few habits help. Ask, do not assume. Say Many Hindus believe, not All Hindus think. Let people describe their own faith. Disagree with ideas, not with a person's worth. These habits are the same ones you have used all year to study religion.

words.d: the teaching to treat others as you would want to be treated, found in many traditions
holding your own view while listening to and treating others fairly

look.title: The Golden Rule in Matthew
look.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
look.prompt: Hillel's version says what not to do. This version says what to do. How are they alike, and how are they different?

check.q: What is the Golden Rule?
choices: Treat others as you would want to be treated
check.why: The Golden Rule, found in many traditions, says to treat others as you would want to be treated.

check.q: In which text does Jesus teach the Golden Rule in the words 'do ye even so to them'?
check.why: Matthew 7:12 in the King James Version contains these words.

check.q: Which sentence shows a respectful habit when talking about religion?
choices: All Hindus think the same thing.
check.why: Saying 'many Hindus believe' attributes the belief and allows for diversity within the tradition.

review.q: Which part of the First Amendment protects a person's right to practice their religion?
review.why: The Free Exercise Clause protects a person's right to practice their religion.

review.q: What did the Court rule in Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972)?
choices: Amish families could end school after eighth grade
review.why: In Yoder, the Court allowed Amish families to end school after eighth grade for reasons of faith.

review.q: What may a public school do, according to Schempp?
choices: Lead daily Bible reading as worship
review.why: Justice Clark wrote that the objective study of religion is allowed in public schools.

review.q: What is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
choices: A 1948 United Nations statement of rights for all people
review.why: The Universal Declaration was adopted by the United Nations in 1948; Article 18 covers religion.

review.q: Why was the 1893 Parliament in Chicago important?
choices: It ended the Thirty Years' War
Many Americans first heard Hindus and Buddhists speak for their own traditions
review.why: At the Parliament, speakers like Vivekananda and Dharmapala spoke for their own traditions.

review.q: Why do estimates of world religions differ?
choices: Some people follow two traditions and questions are asked differently
Every country uses the same census
review.why: Counts differ because of overlapping practice, different questions and different definitions.

choices: People cannot know if God exists
There is no God or gods
review.why: An atheist believes there is no God or gods; an agnostic says it cannot be known.

review.q: Which is an example of religion bringing people together?
choices: Clergy of many faiths marching at Selma in 1965
review.why: At Selma in 1965, Christian and Jewish leaders and others marched together for civil rights.
